title: The Keeper's Daughter
text: Nell had lived in the lighthouse for eleven years, and in all that time she had never once slept through a storm. Her father said this was because she had been born during one, as though the weather had marked her as its own on the very first night of her life.

Tonight the wind came in long, shuddering pushes that made the iron staircase hum. Nell counted the gaps between them the way other children counted sheep. Her father was above her in the lamp room, and she could hear the slow scrape of his boots as he walked his circle around the great glass eye of the light.

At half past two the scraping stopped. Nell sat up. She waited for it to begin again, and when it did not, she was already halfway up the stairs before she had decided to move at all. Her candle went out on the third turn, but she did not need it. She knew the number of steps better than she knew her own age.
She found him at the top, kneeling beside the mechanism with his sleeves pushed back, and the relief that flooded through her was so sudden that it came out as anger. 'You stopped walking,' she said.
'The gear's slipping,' he answered, without looking up. 'Fetch the small oil can, Nell. Quickly now.' And because there was a ship somewhere out in all that black water, she went.

title: Saturday at the Market
text: Otis did not like Saturdays, and he liked market days least of all. It was not the crowds, exactly, nor the smell of frying onions that clung to his jumper for days afterwards. It was that his grandmother expected him to be useful, and being useful meant standing behind the vegetable stall shouting prices at strangers.
'Louder,' she said, without turning round. 'A voice like that will lose us the day.'
Otis tried again. The words came out thin and apologetic, and a woman inspecting the parsnips looked up, smiled kindly, and put them back down.

His grandmother sighed the particular sigh she kept for him. Then she did something unexpected: she came and stood beside him, put one hand flat on the trestle table, and said nothing at all for a full minute. When the next customer approached, she waited. Otis, unable to bear the silence, spoke first — and this time his voice carried right across the square.
'There,' said his grandmother, moving away again. 'You had it all along. You were simply waiting for me to do it for you.'

title: The Causeway
text: The island could be reached on foot for four hours either side of low tide, and Isaac had checked the times twice before setting out. He had written them on the back of his hand in biro: 11:20, and then, underlined, 15:20. Four hours. It had seemed an enormous amount of time when he was standing on the mainland with the whole afternoon ahead of him.

It seemed a good deal less enormous now. The causeway behind him had begun to shine in a way it had not shone an hour ago, and the shine was spreading, the way spilt water spreads across a table — slowly, and then all at once.
He told himself there was no need to hurry. He told himself this several times, quite firmly, and then he began to run.

The water reached the causeway before he did. It came from both sides at once, which was the part nobody had warned him about; he had imagined it creeping in politely from one direction, giving him a chance to outpace it. Instead it simply arrived, cold and unhurried, and closed over the stones as though they had never been there.

There was a wooden refuge box on stilts halfway along, put there for people exactly as foolish as he had been. Isaac climbed the ladder, sat down on the damp bench inside, and watched the last of the path disappear. He was not in any danger. He was, however, going to have to explain this, and that was almost worse.

title: The New Girl
text: For the first three days, nobody could pronounce her name properly, and Marguerite let them all get it wrong. She said nothing at registration when Mr Okafor said 'Margaret'. She said nothing in the dinner queue when a boy with a football under his arm called her 'Margarine' and looked round to see who was laughing.
Her mother asked, on the third evening, how school was going. 'Fine,' said Marguerite, which was true in the way that a photograph of a room is true.

On the fourth day something small happened. A girl called Priya, who had not laughed at the football boy's joke and had not defended her either, leaned across during silent reading and said, quite quietly, 'How do you actually say it?'
Marguerite told her. Priya repeated it, got it slightly wrong, frowned, and tried again. She got it right the second time and then said it a third time, as though filing it away somewhere safe.

It was not a friendship yet. It was not even a conversation, really. But Marguerite found that she was looking forward to silent reading the next day, and that was more than she had felt about anything since the move.
